slides.title: Reticulocyte count
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for · 1/3
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood (hematology EDTA tube); heel-stick capillary blood in newborns  ·  Units: %

What it is used for: The count is most often used to diagnose specific types of anemia, see whether anemia treatment is working, check whether the bone marrow makes enough red cells, and check marrow function after chemotherapy or a bone marrow transplant.

slides.title: Reticulocyte count
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for · 2/3
bullets: It is ordered when other tests (CBC, hemoglobin, hematocrit) show abnormal red cell levels, during radiation or chemotherapy, after a recent bone marrow transplant and for symptoms of anemia. Newborns may be tested for hemolytic disease of the newborn, which can occur with Rh incompatibility between mother and baby.

Physiology: Reticulocytes are immature (still developing) red blood cells made in the bone marrow; they enter the blood and mature into red cells within one to two days. The count checks whether the marrow makes the right amount of red cells as old ones die off.

slides.title: Reticulocyte count
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for · 3/3
bullets: Modern analysers do more than count reticulocytes: they measure maturity by RNA content (the fraction of the youngest cells — IRF), cell volume and haemoglobin content (RET-He or CHr). Names, method and reference ranges depend on the analyser.

slides.title: Reticulocyte count
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Interpreting the result · 1/2
bullets: High: Reticulocytosis (a high count) may mean hemolytic anemia (red cells are destroyed faster than the marrow can replace them), new or ongoing bleeding (the body makes many more red cells to replace those lost), or hemolytic disease of the newborn.

High: IRF is an early marker of marrow activity: after stem-cell transplantation it shows erythroid recovery before the total reticulocyte count does; Dolgov et al. also cite it as an early sign of response to anaemia treatment.

slides.title: Reticulocyte count
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Interpreting the result · 2/2
bullets: Low: A low count may mean iron deficiency anemia, pernicious anemia (a megaloblastic anemia from too little or poorly absorbed vitamin B12 and folate), aplastic anemia (the marrow cannot make enough blood cells), bone marrow failure from infection or cancer, kidney disease or cirrhosis.

Low: Reticulocyte haemoglobin content (RET-He, CHr) indirectly reflects the functional iron available for red cell production over the previous 3–4 days; a low value points to iron-restricted erythropoiesis. The cut-off depends on the analyser and laboratory — use the reference on the report.

slides.title: Reticulocyte count
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 1/4
bullets: Pre-analytics: No special preparation is needed. Adults give a vein sample; in newborns the heel is pricked with a small needle.

Per the WHO phlebotomy guidelines, hematology tests use an EDTA tube (usually purple top): EDTA removes calcium by forming calcium salts. The tube needs a full draw and gentle inversion so the blood mixes thoroughly with the additive — poor mixing can give erroneous results. Cap colors may differ by manufacturer.

Interferences: Reticulocyte counts may be higher during pregnancy; they rise for a short time after moving to a high altitude and return to normal once the body adjusts. Some medicines may increase or decrease the count.

slides.title: Reticulocyte count
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 2/4
bullets: On analysers reticulocytes can be falsely high because of nucleated red cells (NRBCs), red-cell inclusions or fluorescent interference; with an analyser flag or a result that does not fit the clinical picture, check the smear.
Limitations: To understand the result, the provider considers symptoms, history and other blood tests; an abnormal count does not always mean anemia or another condition.

slides.title: Reticulocyte count
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 3/4
bullets: In anaemia the absolute count or a haematocrit-corrected index (CRC, RPI) is used instead of the percentage. Takami (2026) gives approximate adult guides: above about 80×10⁹/L suggests an increased marrow response (bleeding, haemolysis, recovery); below about 20×10⁹/L with severe anaemia suggests markedly impaired erythropoiesis. These are not rigid diagnostic cut-offs.

MSCV (mean sphered cell volume) is reported only by some analysers (per the source, Beckman Coulter). In hereditary spherocytosis MSCV is usually lower than MCV, which helps separate it from thalassaemia; the diagnosis is confirmed with the smear, family studies and other tests.

slides.title: Reticulocyte count
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 4/4
bullets: Manual counting uses a supravital stain (e.g., brilliant cresyl blue) and relates reticulocytes to red cells (traditionally per 1000). Since the 1990s automated flow-cytometric counting has replaced microscopy: it is more accurate and precise, but results are not fully standardised between laboratories.

slides.title: Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH)
slides.eyebrow: Enzymes · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Blood; in certain cases cerebrospinal, peritoneal or pleural fluid

What it is used for: LDH is mainly used to check for tissue damage. It may help diagnose or monitor diseases of the blood (including anemia), liver, lungs, kidneys, heart (including heart attack), pancreas, brain and spinal cord, and help monitor conditions that may worsen over time, such as muscular dystrophy and HIV.

It may also help diagnose certain severe infections, show how serious some cancers are (multiple myeloma, lymphoma, leukemia, testicular cancer, melanoma) and check whether treatment for certain cancers is working.

slides.title: Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH)
slides.eyebrow: Enzymes · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Physiology: LDH (lactate, or lactic acid, dehydrogenase) is an enzyme that helps cells make energy and is found in almost all tissues, with the largest amounts in muscles, liver, kidneys and red blood cells. When disease or injury damages these tissues, the cells release LDH into the blood or other body fluids.

slides.title: Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH)
bullets: High: In general, higher-than-normal LDH usually means some type of tissue damage, usually from disease, infection or injury; more tests may be needed to diagnose the condition.

Low: Lower-than-normal LDH is uncommon and usually not considered a health problem. Taking large amounts of vitamin C or vitamin E, or the rare genetic disorder lactate dehydrogenase deficiency, may cause low levels.

slides.title: Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH)
bullets: Pre-analytics: No special preparation is needed for an LDH blood test. For other fluids (cerebrospinal fluid by lumbar puncture, chest fluid by thoracentesis, abdominal fluid by paracentesis) the provider explains how to prepare.

Interferences: A high LDH does not always mean a condition that needs treatment: intense exercise and certain medicines, including aspirin, can raise it. LDH can also be high if many red blood cells broke open while the sample was collected and tested (hemolysis).

slides.title: Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH)
bullets: Limitations: An LDH test alone cannot show what is damaging tissues or where the damage is, so it is usually done with other tests. The meaning of a result depends on why the test was done, the symptoms and other test results.
If LDH is high, an LDH isoenzyme test, which measures five forms of LDH, may be ordered to help find the type and location of the damaged tissue and how serious the damage is.

slides.title: Total bilirubin
slides.eyebrow: Liver · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood; heel-stick blood in newborns

What it is used for: Used to check liver health, look for the cause of jaundice, find a bile duct blockage, monitor existing liver disease and check how well treatment works. It also helps diagnose disorders in which red blood cells break down too quickly, such as hemolytic anemia.

Commonly used to help diagnose newborn jaundice. Many healthy babies get it because their liver is not yet mature enough; it is usually harmless and clears within a few weeks, but in some cases high bilirubin can lead to brain damage, so infants are often tested as a precaution.

slides.title: Total bilirubin
slides.eyebrow: Liver · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Physiology: Bilirubin is a yellowish substance formed during the normal breakdown of old red blood cells and is found in bile. A healthy liver removes most of it through the bile ducts; if the liver is damaged or the ducts are blocked, bilirubin can leak into the blood, and too much can cause jaundice.

Jaundice arises in three ways: too many red cells break down (prehepatic, haemolytic); the liver is damaged or cannot process bilirubin (hepatic); bilirubin from the liver cannot reach the gut (posthepatic, obstructive — blocked bile ducts).

slides.title: Total bilirubin
bullets: High: Possible causes of high bilirubin (hyperbilirubinemia): hemolytic anemia, liver disease and blockage of the bile ducts.

High: So a raised total bilirubin is fractionated. Mainly indirect (unconjugated) — haemolysis or impaired conjugation such as Gilbert syndrome; direct (conjugated) — hepatocellular disease (e.g., viral or alcoholic hepatitis) or cholestasis/bile-duct obstruction.
Low: Low bilirubin (hypobilirubinemia) is not usually a cause for concern; it may be due to medicines such as antibiotics, birth control pills, sleeping pills and seizure medicines.

slides.title: Total bilirubin
bullets: Pre-analytics: The provider may ask for fasting for several hours before the test. Tell the provider about all medicines taken; stop any only if the provider says so.
Interferences: An abnormal result does not always mean a condition that needs treatment: some medicines, certain foods and strenuous exercise can also raise bilirubin.

Limitations: Normal ranges vary between laboratories and with sex and age (infant or child). Bilirubin is only one measure of liver health; liver function tests, liver protein tests, urine tests, an ultrasound or a liver biopsy may also be needed.

slides.title: Total bilirubin
bullets: When liver test results are abnormal, the provider compares all the measured substances to look for patterns that suggest different types of liver conditions. Liver function tests alone usually cannot diagnose a specific disease.

Urine and stool help tell the types apart. Prehepatic: no bilirubin in urine (unconjugated bilirubin does not pass into urine), much urobilinogen, dark stool. Hepatic: bilirubin in urine, urobilinogen often raised. Posthepatic: bilirubin in urine (dark urine), little or no urobilinogen, pale clay-coloured stool. This is a general pattern — diagnosis relies on the clinical picture and other tests.

slides.title: G6PD (glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood; heel-stick capillary blood in newborns

What it is used for: The test checks for inherited G6PD deficiency: with symptoms of hemolytic anemia (fatigue, pale skin or jaundice, rapid heart rate, shortness of breath, dark or yellow-orange urine); in a newborn whose jaundice does not go away in two weeks and/or has no other cause; or with a family history of G6PD deficiency.

Physiology: G6PD is an enzyme that helps red blood cells work properly. G6PD deficiency is inherited, mainly affects men (women are more often carriers) and is more common in people of African, Mediterranean or Asian descent.

slides.title: G6PD (glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Most people with the deficiency have no symptoms until exposed to a trigger: fava (broad) beans — hemolysis after eating them or inhaling fava pollen is called favism; viral and bacterial infections; certain antibiotics; anti-malaria medicines; NSAIDs such as ibuprofen and aspirin. Red cells are then destroyed faster than they can be replaced — hemolytic anemia.

slides.title: G6PD (glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Interpreting the result
bullets: Low: Lower-than-normal G6PD means G6PD deficiency; symptoms and the risk of hemolytic anemia depend on personal history and exposure to triggers. A slightly low level in a woman may mean she is a carrier (one defective and one normal gene); male children are more likely to develop symptoms than female children.

slides.title: G6PD (glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences
bullets: Pre-analytics: No special preparation is needed. Adults give a vein sample; babies have a heel stick.

Limitations: A man with a normal G6PD level is unlikely to have a deficiency, and anemia may have another cause. If the test was done during an episode of hemolytic anemia, the provider may repeat it in a few weeks.
Most people with G6PD deficiency prevent symptoms by avoiding triggering substances; the provider helps work out which ones to avoid.

slides.title: Hemoglobin electrophoresis
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood; heel-stick capillary blood in newborns
What it is used for: Electrophoresis applies an electric current to a blood sample: normal and abnormal hemoglobin types separate, and each is measured and compared with the normal level.

It is mostly used to help diagnose anemia, sickle cell disease and other hemoglobin disorders: with symptoms, in newborn screening, and in pregnancy when there is a risk of a child with an inherited hemoglobin disorder (family history; thalassemia, for example, is most common in people of Italian, Greek, Middle Eastern, Southern Asian and African descent).

slides.title: Hemoglobin electrophoresis
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Physiology: HbA is the most common hemoglobin in healthy adults. HbF (fetal hemoglobin) is found in unborn babies and newborns and is usually replaced by HbA by age one to two. Abnormal hemoglobin can change red cell size and shape, so cells clump, block blood flow and break down sooner (anemia).

Abnormal types: HbS causes sickle cell disease (stiff, sticky, sickle-shaped cells get stuck in blood vessels, causing pain, infections and other complications); HbC does not carry oxygen well and can cause mild anemia; HbE is mostly found in people of Southeast Asian descent, usually with no or mild anemia symptoms.

slides.title: Hemoglobin electrophoresis
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Interpreting the result
bullets: High: Abnormal levels of hemoglobin types may be a sign of thalassemia (the body does not make enough normal hemoglobin), sickle cell trait (one sickle cell gene; usually no health issues, but the gene can be passed on), sickle cell disease, hemoglobin C disease (mild anemia, sometimes an enlarged spleen and joint pain) or hemoglobin S-C disease. Results may also show whether a disorder is mild, moderate or severe.

slides.title: Hemoglobin electrophoresis
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences
bullets: Pre-analytics: No special preparation is needed. Adults give a vein sample; newborns have a heel stick.
Interferences: A blood transfusion in the last 12 weeks can affect the results — tell the provider.

Limitations: Results are interpreted with symptoms, history and other tests — often a complete blood count and a blood smear. In thalassemia the CBC shows fewer healthy red cells and less hemoglobin, and cells may look smaller depending on the type; genetic testing can help determine the specific type.
If there is a risk of having a child with an inherited hemoglobin disorder, a genetic counselor can explain the disorder and the risk of passing it on.

slides.title: Haemolytic anaemia
bullets: Red cells are destroyed faster than the marrow can replace them. Haemolysis is supported by raised reticulocytes, LDH and unconjugated bilirubin and low haptoglobin; the direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test identifies autoimmune forms, and the smear shows membrane defects and thrombotic microangiopathy.

slides.title: Haemolytic anaemia
rows: Compensatory marrow response; may fail to rise with iron/vitamin deficiency, infection or marrow involvement.
Rises markedly, especially with intravascular haemolysis.

slides.title: Haemolytic anaemia
rows: Most often used to diagnose haemolytic anaemia; falls with haemolysis.
The cornerstone test for autoimmune haemolytic anaemia.
When an enzyme defect is suspected.

slides.title: Haemolytic anaemia
rows: Haemolysis likely; the cause is then sought with the Coombs test and smear.
Intravascular haemolysis (e.g., paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria, prosthetic valve).
Anaemia + thrombocytopenia + haemolysis markers, schistocytes on smear
Possible thrombotic microangiopathy or DIC — urgent evaluation.

slides.title: Haemolytic anaemia
rows: Suspected hereditary spherocytosis: high MCHC, MSCV < MCV, spherocytes on smear
Confirmed with family studies and specific tests.

slides.title: Haemolytic anaemia
bullets: Reticulocytes, LDH, bilirubin and haptoglobin also change outside haemolysis (e.g., haptoglobin is low in liver disease and normally low in infants); in some autoimmune haemolytic anaemia reticulocytes are low.

slides.title: Thalassemia (suspected or trait)
bullets: When symptoms are minor or absent, thalassemia may be suspected from a routine blood test; family history is also assessed.

slides.title: Thalassemia (suspected or trait)
rows: People with thalassemia have fewer healthy red cells and less hemoglobin; depending on the type, red cells may look smaller.
Measures the types of hemoglobin in the blood; helps tell apart conditions caused by hemoglobin problems.
The average size of red blood cells — part of the complete blood count.

slides.title: Thalassemia (suspected or trait)
rows: Determines the specific type of thalassemia.
Low iron may occur with iron-deficiency anemia, another type of anemia, or thalassemia.

slides.title: Thalassemia (suspected or trait)
rows: Hemoglobin ↓ + small red cells, family history
Thalassemia is possible — clarified with special hemoglobin tests and genetic testing.
A1C unexpected or at odds with glucose
A hemoglobin variant (for example, thalassemia in the family) may be affecting it.

slides.title: 1. Is there anaemia?
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Anaemia: step by step
bullets: Defined by haemoglobin. WHO (2024): <120 g/L in non-pregnant women aged 15–65, <130 g/L in men; cut-offs are adjusted for age, pregnancy, altitude and smoking.
First check that the result is genuine — see “Analyser spurious results”.

slides.title: 2. Type by MCV
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Anaemia: step by step
bullets: Low MCV (≈ <80 fL): Microcytic: mostly iron deficiency; thalassaemia → ferritin, iron studies
Normal MCV: Normocytic: acute blood loss, kidney disease, chronic disease, aplastic anaemia → reticulocytes decide
High MCV (≈ >100 fL): Macrocytic: B12 or folate deficiency, liver disease, alcohol, hypothyroidism → B12, folate

slides.title: 3. Marrow response — reticulocytes
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Anaemia: step by step
bullets: High (≈ >80×10⁹/L): Bleeding, haemolysis or recovery after treatment → haemolysis markers
Low (≈ <20×10⁹/L with severe anaemia): Poor production: deficiencies, kidney, marrow disease
Cut-offs are approximate; use the absolute count or a corrected index (CRC, RPI) rather than the percentage.

slides.title: MCV with RDW
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Anaemia: step by step
bullets: MCV ↓, RDW normal: Thalassaemia trait, some anaemia of chronic disease
MCV ↓, RDW ↑: Iron deficiency (ferritin, transferrin saturation)
MCV normal, RDW ↑: Early iron deficiency, mixed deficiency, after transfusion
MCV ↑, RDW ↑: B12 or folate deficiency, myelodysplasia

slides.title: Iron: deficiency or inflammation?
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Anaemia: step by step
bullets: Iron deficiency: Ferritin ↓, iron ↓, transferrin saturation ↓, TIBC usually ↑
Anaemia of inflammation: Iron ↓, TIBC ↓, ferritin normal or ↑
Ferritin cut-off (WHO 2020): Healthy adults <15 µg/L; with inflammation <70 µg/L (with CRP, AGP)

slides.title: Haemolysis markers
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Anaemia: step by step
bullets: Reticulocytes ↑, LDH ↑, indirect bilirubin ↑, haptoglobin ↓.
The Coombs (antiglobulin) test identifies immune haemolysis; spherocytes suggest a membrane defect, schistocytes thrombotic microangiopathy.
A marked LDH rise with haemosiderinuria — intravascular haemolysis.

slides.title: Reference values and decision limits
slides.footnote: The reference interval varies by laboratory, method and population; the laboratory verifies its own interval (verification).

slides.title: Why are newborns often tested for bilirubin?
options: Newborn jaundice always means liver cancer
Many healthy newborns get jaundice because their liver is immature; it is usually harmless, but high bilirubin can sometimes damage the brain
Newborns cannot produce bilirubin, so any amount is abnormal
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: this is why infants are often tested as a precaution.

Basis: MedlinePlus: many healthy babies get jaundice because their livers haven't developed enough; in some cases high bilirubin can lead to brain damage, so infants are often tested as a precaution.

slides.title: Does a high bilirubin result on its own establish liver disease?
options: Yes — a high bilirubin always means liver disease, so other causes and further tests need not be considered
Yes, if the patient is also jaundiced, because jaundice proves the liver is the cause
No — it is only one measure of liver health, and medicines, foods or strenuous exercise can also raise it
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: further tests such as liver function tests, urine tests, ultrasound or biopsy may be needed.

Basis: MedlinePlus: a bilirubin blood test is only one measure of liver health; some medicines, certain foods or strenuous exercise can also raise bilirubin.

slides.title: Many red blood cells broke open while a sample was collected, and LDH is high. How should this be viewed?
options: Broken red blood cells lower LDH, so the true value is even higher
Red blood cells contain a lot of LDH, and their breaking open during collection and testing can give a high LDH
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct. The source names red blood cells among the richest sources of LDH and says LDH can be high in this situation.

Basis: MedlinePlus: LDH can be high if many red blood cells broke open when the sample was collected and tested.

slides.title: Why is an LDH test usually done together with other tests?
options: Because LDH is found only in the heart, and other tests are needed to check other organs
Because LDH cannot be measured in blood and is only estimated from other results
Because LDH alone cannot show what is damaging the tissue or where the damage is
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct. The source gives this as the reason LDH is usually done with other tests.

Basis: MedlinePlus: an LDH test alone cannot show the cause or location of damage, so it is usually done with other tests.

slides.title: What may reticulocytosis indicate, per the source?
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: the marrow replaces the lost cells.

Basis: A rise — hemolytic anemia or bleeding; a fall — iron deficiency, aplastic anemia and others.

slides.title: What are reticulocytes?
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct.

Basis: Immature red cells that leave the marrow and mature in 1–2 days.

slides.title: What does an increase of reticulocytes in peripheral blood indicate:
options: normal blood formation in the bone marrow
increased regenerative function of the bone marrow
chronic blood loss in the patient
breakdown of reticulocytes in peripheral blood

slides.title: The following forms of erythrocytes were found in a peripheral blood smear: macrocytes, megalocytes, erythrocytes with Howell-Jolly bodies and Cabot rings, poikilocytosis. Which anemia can be suspected:
A patient developed signs of anemia three years after gastric resection. Blood test: RBC 2.3×10¹²/L, Hb 92 g/L, color index 1.2, macro- and megalocytosis. Which anemia can be suspected:

A patient has an erythrocyte count of 3500/µL, Hb 70 g/L, color index 0.6. The blood shows marked hypochromia, anisocytosis toward microcytosis. Considering the patient's history of frequent small blood losses, which anemia can be suspected:
Clinical and diagnostic significance of reticulocytes. The IRF (immature reticulocyte fraction) parameter?
bullets: 1. Reticulocytes are young erythrocytes that retain RNA remnants; they mature for 1–3 days in the bone marrow and 1–2 days in the blood; their number reflects the activity of erythropoiesis in the bone marrow.

2. Normal in adults ~0.5–2.5%; because the percentage depends on the erythrocyte count, it is corrected in anemia: RPI (reticulocyte production index) = reticulocyte % × patient Ht / 45; the absolute count is also calculated.
3. Increase: hemolytic anemias, acute/chronic blood loss, treatment effect ("reticulocyte crisis" after giving iron, B12).

slides.title: Clinical and diagnostic significance of reticulocytes. The IRF (immature reticulocyte fraction) parameter?
bullets: 4. Decrease: iron deficiency, anemia of chronic disease, sideroblastic anemia, aplastic anemia, MDS, B12/folate deficiency (before treatment), aplastic crisis in hemolytic anemia (parvovirus B19), hydroxyurea.

5. IRF is the ratio of immature (high-RNA) reticulocytes to total reticulocytes; measured on the analyzer by fluorescence intensity. The earliest sign of bone marrow regeneration: used to monitor recovery after chemotherapy and bone marrow transplantation.
6. Reticulocyte hemoglobin (CHr/Ret-He) reflects iron available for erythropoiesis; <28 pg is a good predictor of iron deficiency.

slides.title: Methods of determining reticulocytes?
bullets: 1. Reticulocyte RNA is stained with supravital dyes (new methylene blue or brilliant cresyl blue) as a network/granules: blood is mixed with the dye and incubated, a smear is made, and under oil immersion the proportion of reticulocytes among erythrocytes is counted.
2. The drawback of the manual method is low reproducibility (few cells are counted, observer-dependent); therefore it is rarely used now.

3. Automated method – flow cytometry: staining with a fluorescent dye that binds RNA (for example thiazole orange), measurement on a laser analyzer; percentage, absolute count, IRF and CHr/Ret-He are reported.

slides.title: Methods of determining reticulocytes?
bullets: 4. Interpreting the result: normal ~0.5–2.5%; in anemia, correction by RPI = reticulocyte % × Ht/45; the absolute count is also taken into account.
5. Significance: increased in hemolysis and blood loss (bone marrow response), decreased in hypoproliferative anemias (iron, B12/folate deficiency, aplasia); assessing treatment effect.

slides.title: Hemolytic anemias. Clinical and laboratory parameters?
bullets: 1. Hemolytic anemia is shortened erythrocyte survival; intravascular (hemoglobinemia, hemoglobinuria, hemosiderinuria) and extravascular (in spleen/liver macrophages, spherocytes) hemolysis.

2. Classification: inherited – membranopathies (hereditary spherocytosis), enzymopathies (G6PD, pyruvate kinase deficiency), hemoglobinopathies (sickle cell, thalassemias); acquired – autoimmune (warm/cold antibodies), alloimmune (incompatible blood, hemolytic disease of the newborn), microangiopathic (TTP, HUS, DIC), infectious (malaria), toxic, PNH.

slides.title: Hemolytic anemias. Clinical and laboratory parameters?
bullets: 3. General laboratory signs: reticulocytosis, LDH↑, indirect bilirubin↑, haptoglobin↓ (the most sensitive); in intravascular hemolysis free Hb, hemoglobinuria, hemosiderinuria.
4. The smear points to the cause: spherocytes (hereditary spherocytosis, warm AIHA), schistocytes (microangiopathy), sickle and target cells, Heinz bodies/"bite" cells (G6PD), parasites.

5. Depending on the cause, special tests: with suspected immune hemolysis the direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test; in inherited forms, membrane, enzyme (e.g. G6PD) and hemoglobin studies – in a specialized laboratory.
